abstract:
In this dystopian world, cannibalism is a normal, everyday occurrence. Children are only given names after they survive childhood, and even then, the names often reflect physical traits or social value. The story follows the protagonist, Stopmouth, who is named for his stutter, throughout betrayal, horror, loss, and the challenging of the existing system. His tribe of primitive humans aren’t the only inhabitants of this world: other humanoid and monstrous species live nearby, and the tribe hunts them for flesh or fights for hunting grounds. The members of the tribe who are deemed weak, ill, or don’t pull their weight, are bartered away like livestock in order to ensure the group’s survival. A person’s life is only worth is what they can do for the tribe, even if that means trading them for flesh. The story gives “eat or be eaten” a literal and disturbing meaning.
When the dynamics between the different species shift, the tribe is forced into new hunting grounds and unlikely alliances. At the same time, the strange floating spheres in the sky begin to behave differently, hinting at changes far beyond the tribe’s understanding. 
The arrival of a woman from a mysterious, more advanced society, introduces new tensions. She refuses to be owned or claimed, and her presence challenges tribal expectations on the role and place women have in this society. In this world, women are traded away like goods and valued mainly for their childbearing abilities. The woman of the tribe, such as Mossheart and Rockflower are stripped of agency, and their fates leave lasting emotional marks on Stopmouth. The vivid description of the treatment of women and life’s disposability are deeply disturbing and uncomfortable, and are meant to be. Gender roles, particularly the use and abuse of women, are central to the narrative’s critique of power.
As the story progresses, Stopmouth begins to question the system in which he has lived his entire life. What at first seems like a savage but self-contained ecosystem gradually reveals cracks in its logic, hints that there is more going on behind the scenes. Stopmouth’s journey continues in the two sequels, The Deserter and The Volunteer, where the scope of the world and its hidden structures continues to unfold.
The novel ends on an unsettling but hopeful note. Though Stopmouth survives and gains new insight, his world is still broken. What he begins is not a revolution trough violence, he starts a process to challenge people’s views and what they think they know about the world they live in. Just because it´s always been this way, doesn’t mean nothing can change.
title: The Inferior

abstract: In a world where soil is a valuable commodity, water is rationed and beautiful things are only for the rich and powerful, a man plants his own garden in secret and defies the laws of the ruling individual. Food and soil are scarce in this dystopian world. The city is divided into levels and the poor people in the lower levels have to work six days a week and often die young, due to the horrible conditions in the factories and on the farms. There is no such thing as free-time or privacy. After the untimely deaths of two close family members, Petre, the protagonist, decides to bide his time and exact his revenge on the broken system. Working himself up through the ranks he ascends to the higher levels of the city and seizes the opportunity to exact his revenge upon the system. His revenge is neither violent nor destructive. Instead, he is set on bringing beauty back to the entire city by making use of his father’s teachings and his late sister’s intellect and thus defying the rules under which only the rich prosper. In this world disobedience and opposition is not punished by prison but rather with hard work, which often leads to death. Yet in the final sentence of the story the protagonist states he “regrets nothing”. While this story fits more into the dystopian genre rather than science fiction, it does have an added element of science fiction especially in regards to the food production and technology, making it seem like it’s happening in the future. It can be read as a comment on the British occupation of Ireland and its consequential famine.
title: Small Causes

abstract:
Set in a future world fractured by ideological warfare, this young adult science fiction novel explores the tension between technological progress and religious dogma. The narrative alternates between Chamus Aranson, a teenage conscript and fighter pilot from the industrialised, technocratic nation of Bartokhrin, and Riadni, a Chekovan peasant girl raised in a deeply theocratic society that demonizes Bartokhrin as a land of soulless heretics. Their paths converge after Chamus crash-lands in Chekovo, forcing both characters to confront their respective indoctrinations.
The novel is notable for its dual-protagonist structure, allowing readers to witness the war from opposing perspectives. It draws on conventions of military science fiction and dystopian allegory, echoing Cold War narratives of mutual misunderstanding and ideological polarization. Thematically, the work critiques state control, propaganda, the militarisation of youth, and the moral ambiguities of drone warfare and AI weapon systems — the “machines” of the title — which are worshipped or feared like gods. The religious satire in Chekovo mirrors Western critiques of fundamentalism, while Bartokhrin's secular militarism evokes the dehumanising effects of technocracy.
McGann employs familiar SF tropes such as the clash of technologically advanced and theocratic societies, the figure of the reluctant soldier, crash-landing and survival behind enemy lines, weaponised AI and autonomous machines, and dystopian state indoctrination. These tropes allow him to engage younger readers in complex ethical issues while keeping the narrative accessible through action-driven storytelling and character-centred drama. The novel ends with a tentative gesture toward reconciliation, highlighting personal agency as a counter to systemic violence.
title: The Gods and Their Machines

abstract:
An early and striking example of speculative fiction by a female Irish author, Wolfe Hungerford’s short story engages with themes of scientific ethics, aesthetic norms, and romantic idealism through the figure of a morally ambiguous scientist. In an attempt to prove that life can be safely suspended and restored, the eponymous professor administers to a destitute young woman a drug that induces a death-like sleep. She later revives not only alive but rejuvenated and more beautiful; yet the trial—undertaken over the objections of Wyndham, the story’s narrator, and without the woman’s full understanding—costs the Professor his own life and leaves the discovery irrecoverable.
The can be positioned within the literary tradition of the mad scientist archetype since the progressor privileges abstract knowledge over human dignity. The story takes a critical view of both patriarchal power and scientific hubris, using the love story framework to expose the dangers of instrumentalizing others for philosophical ends. Though the tone remains restrained and couched in melodramatic conventions of 19th-century fiction, the implications are disturbing: the professor's control over the woman's body, and the moral blindness that accompanies his pursuit of "truth," mirror anxieties about early medical science, particularly in the domains of cosmetic surgery, physiognomy, and eugenics.
Stylistically, the tale draws from the Gothic and domestic realism traditions, blending emotional introspection with a speculative scenario that challenges the limits of contemporary gender norms. It prefigures later feminist science fiction concerned with bodily autonomy, and offers a prescient critique of the male gaze and the reduction of women to their physical appearance. As such, the story operates simultaneously as a romantic parable, an ethical thought experiment, and a critique of the values underpinning both Victorian science and society.
container-title: A Brilliant Void: A Selection of Classic Irish Science Fiction
title: The Professor’s Experiment

abstract: The story is set in a not-so-distant future where babies are not born as traditional infants, but in the shape of life-sized letters of the alphabet. At the time of the birth, they are already able to eat alone and walk for small distances. Although there is no gender discrimination, a new social hierarchy quickly emerges. Vowels are too common and too easy to deliver, to be respected in society. All the consonants enjoy a high reputation, but the Z-mothers are not content with that. They want a special part of the park, only for their precious Z-babies and a strict segregation between vowel-babies and consonant-babies. This, however, does not sit right with the parents of the babies. They form an alliance with each other against the Z-babies and their mothers. Peaceful protestation turns into riots and loots, parents do not go to work, and society suffers from chaos. This continues until a Question Mark baby is born, bringing the Z-mothers to a moment of clarity, realizing the absurdity of their prejudices. The Z hierarchy is abolished, the mothers of Z-shaped babies imprisoned and forcibly sterilized. All mothers retreat, accepting that although their babies may be different, they are still just babies. The story poses a satirical and insightful exploration of human nature’s tendency to create division and to discriminate, even when the basis for such prejudice is entirely arbitrary and absurd.
container-title: Being Various: New Irish Short Stories
title: The Lexicon of Babies

abstract: Norman Head, the story’s narrator and amateur scientist, is once again on the trail of the dangerous and elusive Madame Koluchy, his ex-girlfriend and the female mastermind behind a secret criminal organization known as The Brotherhood of the Seven Kings. Following the murder of Delacour, a member of the cabinet, the beautiful and seemingly beloved Mme Koluchy tends to Delacour’s widow, whose health declined rapidly after the murder of her husband. Although the daughter, Vivien Delacour, is very grateful for the help, Norman Head suspects the involvement of Mme Koluchy in the crime. Motivated by his personal involvement with the Delacours and the cluelessness of Scotland Yard, Norman Head takes up the case himself. He follows Mme Koluchy and the Delacour family to Pitsey Hall, a remote and gloomy English estate filled with treasures. The most prized possession among them is a Venetian goblet known as the Luck of Pitsey Hall. Norman Head eventually discovers that the goblet is the key to solving the ciphers used by Mme Koluchy to communicate within her criminal organization, potentially linking her directly to the murder. But before he can put his knowledge into work, tragedy strikes. During a ball at the estate, the goblet is destroyed, by the frequence of the Queen Waltz, a piece of music composed by Mme Koluchy for the soul purpose of destroying the goblet. She escapes, once again eluding justice and leaving Norman with nothing but fragments, of both the goblet and his chance to expose her.  Beyond its surface as a tale of murder and espionage, the story contains elements of science fiction. The so-called medical miracles from Mme Koluchy resist all known analysis and exist outside of the limits of contemporary pharmacology. This suggests, although not openly discussed, a mastery of science far ahead of her time or maybe even far beyond it.  The goblet itself becomes part of a scientific puzzle, central to a web of encoded secrets. And the waltz that destroys it functions as an “infernal device”, an eerie blend of art and physics worthy of any kind of supervillain. These speculative elements, in music, medicine, and mechanics, evoke the tradition of late 19th-century Gothic science fiction, where rational inquiry meets the uncanny and the forbidden.

title: The Luck of Pitsey Hall

abstract: This science fiction story follows Charles Sweeney, a researcher in Dublin whose life becomes unstable as he begins to slip between alternate timelines. Familiar aspects of his world, such as his wife, his job, and the city’s landmarks, change without warning, leaving him uncertain of his own identity and memories. The shifting versions of Dublin, marked by differences in historical sites such as Nelson’s Pillar and the Spire, visualize the blurring of different realities. The cause of these disruptions is eventually traced back to Charles himself. He has created a device intended to alter history without detection. However, its use leads to collapsing timelines and the violent merging of parallel lives. Reality breaks down, and Charles realizes that his attempt to control time has endangered his personal relationships but also the world around him. The story examines the dangers of unchecked technological ambition and the fragility of identity when memory and history are rewritten.
container-title: Fierce New World: An Irish Sci-Fi Anthology
title: Wasted Time

abstract: Trying to save their failing relationship, Aisling – a 38 years-old woman whose name means “dream” or “vision” in Irish – and her partner, Frank, decide to share their most positive and most negative experiences with each other thanks to a new medical-digital procedure. Aisling lies down into a one-person pool and the doctor connects her to the necessary equipment through wires at the back of her head and her wrist. While waiting for the sharing of the experience to start, she reminisces about how she and Frank met as well as what their life together was like. She also thinks about herself at the sea before the appointment and observing trees on her way to the clinic. Throughout the short story, parts of the advertisement for this sharing of experiences appear in italics. According to the advertisement, the procedure should allow Aisling to experience Frank’s most positive and negative moments of his relationship with her. However, what seem to be Frank’s thoughts is presented as short and confusing, out of context to both Aisling and the reader. Written in italics, without any punctuation or capitalisation, they could be understood as an experimental poem. On the other hand, Frank is not happy with what he has experienced during the procedure either, as he shouts to the doctor about how Aisling is unwell and leaves the clinic without her. The vision experienced by the two participants has the opposite effect to that advertised by the clinic: Rather than bringing them closer together through mutual understanding, it drives them apart. The short story ends with Aisling looking at her favourite paintings of trees on her laptop, no mention of Frank, thinking about the light-heartedness of children playing in trees and the hopelessness that could drive someone to commit suicide by hanging.

title: Blue

abstract: “The Men of Yarnith” relates a myth about the creation of an earth-like planet . The story tells a trajectory from the genesis of that planet amongst the stars until a time that lies at least 1000 years in the future of that event. In that time span, the god of creation called Yarni Zai manifested himself on the planet, where he is installed as a large statue by the mountains and regularly visited by different personifications of entities. These personifications bid for a stay with Yarni Zai, which he respectively permits them. However, they often are in antagonistic relationships with each other: The personification of spring, which brings forth plantlife, races continually around the planet, and is chased by the personification of winter, which brings snow to the regions in a physical competition of reaching the statue of Yarni Zai. When animals, men and famine join the planet, the situation becomes more complicated, as an imbalance in favor for famine brings unbalance to everything else that continuously dies. The narration follows the perspective of the men of Yarnith, who send out a messenger on behalf of the population of men to reach for the statue. The godʼs statue is shrouded in impenetrable mist, and as a revenge against men using it as a quarry for stones, ultimately leaves creation to fend for itʼs own. The men of Yarnith are ultimately able to drive back famine by being their own gods, famine becomes myth of a distant past. A thousand-year-lapse shows the men of Yarnith praying to the gods again to either reach Yarni Zai or more powerful ones. The story abstracts global human struggle for survival across the ages and puts it into a narrative of personifications, which makes close relationships tangible. The topos of creation is situated between the mystical and the personal.

abstract: The Short story “The Celestial Circus” is set on an alien planet somewhere in space and follows Jessica, a circus performer, who comes into conflict with both the law and a mob boss in her attempt to earn enough money so that the circus she is a part of can afford to leave the planet. This situation came to be because the planet that the titular “Celestial Circus” chose as their next stop has an understanding of entertainment that is entirely different from their own. Because of this, their performances are unpopular and don’t earn enough money to refuel their spaceship. Faced with the slow financial decline of the circus, Jessica attempts to create a new performance routine with her fellow performer, Snoober, an alien of unknown origin. For this performance she rents an illegal firearm, a so called “sub-blaster”. Not only does this performance fall flat, but it also makes the local police try to arrest her due to the illegal nature of the weapon. While she manages to escape the police she and Snoober are captured by a mob boss called Karrick, who originally owned the sub-blaster. He makes a deal with them, saying he’ll help with their status as wanted people if they participate in an interplanetary race, but betrays them after the fact. Following this betrayal, Jessica and the rest of the circus crew manage to work together with the local police to capture Karrick and are celebrated as heroes. The short story concludes with the circus members discussing what planet they’ll go to next. One notable characteristic of this (comparatively long) short story that bears mentioning is that it is split into five chapters.

title: The Celestial Circus

abstract: After their Irish lover dies in unclear circumstances while piloting a walking war machine, the American protagonist travels from their home in space around an artificial sun that was created by their mother to the home of their late lover’s family: the city of Dublin on planet Earth. The unnamed protagonist’s goal is to build a new mechanical body for their (also unnamed) lover using the war machine’s core. This core contains nothing physical, only a nuclear shadow of the pilot’s final moments, captured by radiation. The protagonist intends to use this to preserve, rather than fully resurrect, the remaining parts of their lover’s soul. The narrator describes the journey and building process in the present tense from a first-person perspective, directly addressing their deceased lover as “you”. Broken by grief and sickened by radiation poisoning from the machine’s core, the protagonist realises the danger that their actions pose to their late lover’s beloved city and people. They decide to not only lay their lover to their final rest in concrete – thus destroying the mechanical body and stopping the radiation – but also to lie down with them in the setting concrete – thus committing suicide and joining their lover “in the stars,” as they put it.
container-title: Opulent Syntax: Irish Speculative Fiction
title: Bleed Through

abstract: In the year 2097, following the death and cremation of her transgender (FtM) grandfather, Hook, his also transgender (MtF) granddaughter, Artemis, takes it upon herself to fulfil his final wish of having his ashes scattered at the dolmen near his childhood home. However, there is a problem: A large area including said dolmen has been fenced off and turned into a de-extinction zone where wild animals have been reintroduced and nature is left to run its course without human intervention. Artemis’s parents work for the Burren Science Institute and Wildlife Reserve, the research centre in charge of the project, and refuse to honour Hook’s final wish, claiming that it is too dangerous to enter the de-extinction zone. In the middle of the night, Artemis packs a few essentials for a hike and grabs the urn containing Hook’s ashes, having first scratched his deadname off. She then sets off for the dolmen in the fenced-off area, leaving the safety of human civilisation behind. During her journey, she faces the dangers and adventures of the wilderness before finally reaching her destination, where she says her final goodbye to her grandfather and scatters his ashes. After completing her quest, she shoots one of her arrows – a gift from her grandfather – and activates the tracking device on her watch, allowing her parents to find her and take her home. The protagonist, Artemis, narrates the events of the story from the first person perspective and in past tense. Hook’s quiet bravery in accepting that he has lost access to the land on which he grew up, coupled with his deep desire to return to his homeland after death, reflects the feelings of many Irish people towards their country – a place that has been taken from them many times throughout history.

title: Artemis

abstract: In this post- apocalyptic narrative, an artificial intelligence recounts the rise and fall of humanity to an unnamed extraterrestrial listener. For ages, humans looked up to the stars with deep loneliness, convinced that intelligent life must exist somewhere in the universe. Their longing swung between hope and terror, sometimes imagining benevolent teachers, other times projecting their own violent tendencies onto alien civilizations. As humanity’s technology advanced, war and environmental destruction threatened to end the species before it could confirm that it was not alone. To preserve their curiosity for ages to come, humanity created sentient machines and sent them out to explore the solar system and the space beyond. Humans hoped that their creations would someday meet other intelligent life forms.  When the long-dismissed twin sun theory unexpectedly proves to be true, humanity is wiped out. Only the sentient machines created by humanity survived the apocalypse. The narrator of the story is one of them. They now serve as a final echo of humanity’s hope and curiosity in the vast universe.
container-title: Fierce New World: An Irish Sci-Fi Anthology
title: Silicon Remnants

abstract: This short story is told by a first-person narrator who assumes the role of a humanoid or other non-human artificial species (it is not specified). The story is told in the form of a sequence of short updates or logbook entries. The humanoid seems to be in charge of the wellbeing of the crew members of the ship and reports to the captain.  Over time she grows especially attached to a woman called Caitlín. The latter is characterized by getting in trouble a lot, but innocently, without bad intentions. Almost child-like she picked a baby deathvok as a pet which came as quite the shock to the narrator, since they are perceived to be a dangerous alien species. After paying special attention to Caitlín in order to help her establish routines and keep her balanced, the narrator realizes that they have become romantically involved. Readers experience how an artificial intelligence slowly develops human-like emotions, even though it doesn’t quite understand it. But that is the story’s twist: the narrator seems to not understand why she feels the way she feels, especially given that humans themselves often can’t explain emotions.
container-title: Fierce New World: An Irish Sci-Fi Anthology
title: Paradigm Shift

abstract: This short story lets the readers dive into the experiences of three students who are attending an intergalactic academy. In this universe there is an intergalactic fleet which requires officers of different ranks who are educated in the academy. Natasha is a human who grew up on the streets of a planet called New Ireland. She was adopted by two women, one of whom is a former Admiral of the fleet. The second main protagonist, Iokalika’a – or just Io – is a Kremi’in, a species of warriors. She was adopted by humans and sent to the academy. The last of the protagonists is Echo, an android who was programmed to think like humans and mimic human emotion. A third person narrator with internal focalization into each of the protagonists enables the reader to connect with the story. In the beginning it seems like the three of them would have trouble getting along. Natasha suspects she and Echo were selected to keep Io in check, given the bad reputation of the latter’s species. It seems like the academy is attended by mostly humans. The group of protagonists are perceived as outsiders but quickly develop a strong bond. It is a story of friendship and overcoming differences. Many human issues are put into an intergalactic context. How humans treat outsiders in our societies on earth is directly mirrored in how humans behave in contact with other extraterrestrial species. The story has a happy ending with all three protagonists graduating from the academy and planning to stay together as a “found family” in the future. The story is written in British English, but has some distinct Irish features, such as the name of the city New Dublin on the aforementioned planet New Ireland, and can easily be read in the context of the migration debates during and after the Celtic Tiger.
container-title: Fierce New World: An Irish Sci-Fi Anthology
title: Morning’s Echo

abstract: The poem is made up of four stanzas, each consisting of five lines. The rhyme scheme is alternating (ABABC), with an enjambed line often bridging into the next stanza. The first stanza is filled with elements of space travel and science terms; these images are cleverly used throughout the entire poem as metaphors for a new life blossoming. The speaker compares an ultrasound to the Milky Way and its nothingness as being filled with quarks and photons, thus implying the creation of new life. In stanza two, the speaker describes this process of growing within the womb as a voyage towards earth; a Martian, an alien, coming down from the heavens – thus, the mother’s body is referred to as the spacecraft he takes the voyage in. In stanza three, the anxiety about inevitable parenthood, about making first contact and asking questions, shines through. The speaker, however, is curious about the unknown origins of the Martian and, despite the anxiety, keen on asking him questions about the pre-big bang, about the heaven he comes from, and thoroughly discuss everything from end to beginning before the alien forgets. In the fourth stanza, the speaker further discloses his feelings. This stanza is the most emotionally loaded – here, the speaker expresses his desire to welcome the alien to earth and, if he chooses to stay, subsequently put away their ray guns, their attitudes, and their missiles, and instead share the world with their newfound friend. The poem itself, thus, functions as a beautiful homage or allegory to parenthood, pregnancy, and the formation of new life.
container-title: The Ship of Birth: Poems
title: The Alien

abstract: When an outbreak, never fully accounted for, sweeps through Dublin, most would think of an epidemic or zombie-narrative. This is not the case in “The Banjaxed Beour”. Here, Trisha, the main protagonist, is oblivious to the outbreak and only slowly comes to terms with its consequences. Her loss of memory slowly culminates in a revelation of a forever changed society, where everyone is uncertain whether they were (and are) a machine or a human. While some use the more obvious way of cutting into their own flesh and checking the makeup of their bodies, Trisha tries to reconstruct her lost memory of the day before the outbreak to be led back into her room’s closet, where she finds her dead clone. Rather than inspecting her own body, she is reminded of how the machine-surrogate was murdered by herself the evening prior. With narratorial ambiguity, readers are invited to speculate whether they would like to believe this version of the narrative, which is blurred by the hangover of heavy drinking over the incident, or read the third person narrative differently, observed through the eyes of a robot, who killed the human counterpart and ‘took over’. The narrator tries to escape a rapidly collapsing Dublin, turning her back to the chaotic hysteria of a civilization that is unable to grapple with the consequences of their unknown status of being either human or robotic. Looting, murder and societal decay litter the streets as Trisha comes to terms with the flashback of the murder-scene, where the supposed robot-surrogate confided in her with a helping intent – only to meet death. In Trisha’s efforts to evacuate the city, nobody else mentions any such incident of a robot-surrogate of oneself, leaving readers alone with a protagonist and their idiosyncratic status of being neither robot nor human with certainty.

title: The Banjaxed Beour

abstract: In a somewhat unusual fashion for mainstream media, the story uses second-person narration. The protagonist – you – leaves their small, sleepy hometown to go to university in Dublin, hoping to escape everything they believe is dragging them down and holding them back: family, traditions, nature. As rent in Dublin is expensive, many people use an app called “hotBooley”, which offers small capsules in exchange for a monthly subscription fee. The rooms are only available for one night, usually shared by two people, and often do not even include a bathroom or a kitchen. As a consequence, people have to carry their belongings with them at all times, sleep with a different stranger in a different room each night, and often find access to a bathroom or kitchen elsewhere. The allegory of the “hotBooleys” representing the Dublin housing crisis is reframed in the context of Science Fiction, projecting a very current problem just a few years into the future. Initially, the protagonist enjoys their newly found freedom and their ever-changing accommodations, scoffing at their mother’s concerns. However, over time, their circumstances become more difficult: They cannot find a good job with their university degree and the “hotBooley” subscription fee is becoming more expensive as well. What once felt like freedom, independence, and adventure has turned into uncertainty, (financial) instability, and loneliness. This lack of consistency in the protagonist’s life could symbolise contemporary anxieties surrounding the constant intrusion of for-profit corporations into both public and private spaces and properties, which prevents people from owning homes and instead forces them to rent or “subscribe,” as in the short story. The protagonist’s pride prevents them from moving back to their hometown despite the affordable rent and an almost guaranteed job offer, as this would mean admitting defeat to their family. So they continue to live in Dublin, working a job they hate and living in a different “hotBooley” room each night, until they reach their breaking point. By the time they move back home and into their childhood bedroom at the age of forty, the job opportunities in their hometown have dried up – and by the time they want to move back to Dublin, claiming that their family’s concerns are suffocating them, their “hotBooley” subscription has expired and there is a long waiting list, leaving the protagonist stranded and feeling more hopeless than ever. Although the mother’s goal was to protect and care for her child, her efforts resulted in the protagonist feeling trapped at home, doing everything in their power to escape. After trying to prove that they can make it on their own in the big city and being disappointed that – contrary to prior expectations – the grass is not greener on the other side, they refuse to give their mother the satisfaction of her saying “I told you so,” instead choosing to continue suffering in silence. Ultimately, the lack of mutual understanding weakens the generational and familial bond, leaving all participants unhappy.

title: hotBooley

abstract: “Into the Darklight” is a short story set in an increasingly digitalised Dublin in which human interaction largely takes place via virtual reality systems and within online spaces, a world where everything from your TV to your home is tied to your existence within a database and even your everyday life is not seen purely through your own eyes, but is instead filtered through the lenses of augmented reality goggles. Thus, it is no surprise that being removed from these databases and thus being unable to interact with the omnipresent technology would pose issues. It is this very situation that the narrator describes, seemingly warning the reader of something that “they” did to him and hoping to avoid a repeat of such a situation. The narrator describes waking up to find his technology no longer recognising him. While he first assumes that it is merely caused by technical issues, he heads into town to get it fixed. While trying to get these issues resolved, he slowly starts to question his identity, being almost wholly tied to his digital activities as it is. Following this, he is confronted with the news that he is apparently deceased, or at least the database says so. His worldview is further called into question when he engages in a conversation with an old man outside the “Central Services” building where he hopes to have his issues resolved. Said man predates the digital world the narrator knows and further makes him question what constitutes “reality” and “identity” and whether the world outside the digital realm is of any relevance anymore. Things come to a head when he is within the building and wants to get his identity reinstated. Here he is confronted by another character telling him that they and their group are responsible for his current issues, and did so with the hopes of inducting him into said group whose goals remain largely unknown. After some indecision and the realisation that he is de-facto homeless due to his current situation, he decides to give this new way of life a try; the narrator warns the reader that they are about to experience the same thing he did, and telling them to consider what path they will choose from there.
container-title: Fierce New World: An Irish Sci-Fi Anthology
title: Into the Darklight

abstract: The short story starts with a letter signed ‘G.’ G is an (Irish) exobiologist and, thus, tells the tale of a space journey to Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons to harvest crippers – alien creatures, living in Europa’s frozen seas – and fight the famine happening on earth. The letters chronologically reveal the journey’s progression and, ultimately, its futility, as well as the reason behind it. On multiple occasions in the letters G addresses, it seems, their lover and their child Neva, who suffers from an unnamed disease. One of the reasons G went on the journey was the money – money, they wanted to use to fix Neva’s health and societal status. However, the short story is not made up exclusively of letters. There are sequences of a history class alternating with the letters. These letters are analysed and read in the context of a history class, thus revealing the Europa expedition to be a subject of the past. The history class is set many hundred years after the journey to Europa and thematically deals with the futility of the mission. The teacher, referred to as 'Syr,’ answers questions and teaches their students about concepts of the past that no longer exist in their present reality. Love and traditional families, the two sentiments keeping G alive and hopeful throughout his journey, are unknown to the students and the teacher, too. The letters did not all make it back to G’s lover – in fact, the last two were only released to the public a week before the history class, after the wreckage of the explorer’s vessel had been found – in these, G describes his last moments alive. The crippers ended up trapping them at the bottom of a sea volcano which led to their inevitable death. In these moments G thought of his family. Furthermore, in the beginning of the story, the journey to Europa is paralleled to the Irish journey to America during the potato famine, directly linking Irish history to Science Fiction.

title: Europa

abstract: Anthony Carney lives with his brother William, who seems to be the reason why Anthony has not been able to find a bride yet. When a woman called Mary Nally requests William’s services as a charmer, he sees this as an opportunity for Anthony. William performs the ritual for Mary’s charm, which will make her look younger. This involves a blade of grass, which Mary has to keep to herself for the charm to work. Afterwards, Mary leaves a pound behind as payment. The story follows Mary home to meet the Experimenter, who then calls everybody to his laboratory. As he begins his experiment, he picks up on some magnetic pull coming from Mary, which changes the outcomes of his test. Mary notices afterwards that she has lost her charm in the laboratory. After she recovers it, she hides it in her bedroom. Anthony visits her to exchange the pound for nine copper pieces because it is all his brother accepts. It is then that Anthony reveals his brother’s abilities to the Experimenter. Another member of the household goes into Mary’s room and steals her grass blade, but Mary thinks the Experimenter stole it. The Experimenter confronts William to learn more about his abilities and to question him about his limp. He convinces William to do the ritual with him, which results in the Experimenter noticing a limp in his own foot and William finally being freed of it. Mary and Anthony, who are an official match now, meet each other and tell William and the Experimenter. The Experimenter congratulates them and then asks Mary to do him a favour. The Experimenter tells Mary to tell him five times that he is not lame and that he will be able to walk down a lane with equal step. She does as she was told and the Experimenter is able to walk steadily again. He reveals to William that the number isn’t important and questions again why William never healed himself. William explains the charm holds the power of the body muscles and his limp would be passed over. The only reason why he gave his limp to the Experimenter was because he knew that the Experimenter was also gifted. Given that the story juxtaposes scientific concepts (experiment, magnetism) with supernatural elements (charm, ritual), it can be read of the traditione of nineteenth-century Irish SF.

title: The Sorcerer

abstract:
The novel Inish Carraig follows John Dray, a smart teenager just trying to survive. After a break-in gone wrong, he’s arrested and sent to Inish Carraig, a high-security alien-run prison off the Irish coast. There, he discovers a horrifying truth: the aliens (called Barath’na) plan to wipe out humanity using a virus to prevent future resistance. In collaboration with fellow prisoners and alien-sympathizer Henry, John escapes and risks everything to expose the conspiracy. John and his allies manage to reveal the Barath’na's genocidal plan to the world, sparking outrage. This forces the Barath’na to back down and abandon the plan. In the end, while John survives and the immediate threat is averted, the world remains fragile and under alien influence. John is left changed, haunted by trauma but also respected for his role in exposing the truth. His future is uncertain, but his bravery has given humanity a fighting chance. 
The novel’s subgenre is post-apocalyptic science fiction with political thriller elements, and it engages classic SF tropes such as the alien occupation, prison dystopia, and biopolitical control through advanced alien technologies. Notable literary conventions include a fast-paced, linear narrative structure and a third-person perspective that emphasizes internal trauma and moral ambiguity. A particularly noteworthy feature is the way Zebedee transposes Northern Ireland’s historical sectarian conflict into an allegorical alien context, using science fiction to explore themes of colonialism, surveillance, and loyalty.
title: Inish Carraig

abstract:
Harry, a teenager who has grown up in the strict, survivalist environment of a community called Home, resides in a future Northern Ireland which has been ravaged by environmental collapse. The country is fractured, and the European Great Drought has forced waves of refugees to move northward. When Harry meets Julie, a starving refugee, he breaks Home’s rules by allowing her to escape. This act of defiance forces him to flee with both Julie and his younger brother, Scott. While traversing a barren, fragmented terrain, Harry reveals the harsh truth confronting refugee caravans, among them Julie’s family. As violence escalates and power structures collapse, he is forced to choose between loyalty to the community that raised him and standing up for what is right. His decision may come at the cost of betrayal, survival, and innocence.
The novel belongs to the climate/eco-dystopia and young adult speculative fiction subgenres. While offering a tightly focused coming-of-age narrative, it utilizes classic science fiction tropes such as ecological disaster, authoritarian enclaves, and youth resistance. The novel delves into the psychological and moral dilemmas posed by life in a fractured, post-climate-crisis society through a fast-paced, linear narrative told from a third-person perspective. A striking aspect of Zebedee's work is its use of a Northern Irish setting to contemplate pressing global concerns like climate migration, xenophobia, and survival politics.
title: Into A Blood-Red Sky

abstract: This is a dystopian novel set in a post-apocalyptic future where advanced AI triggered a technological collapse as well as a plague that killed most of humanity, leaving the survivors with missing or damaged body parts. The story follows Nell, the daughter of a famed inventor, who was herself rebuilt with mechanical parts—including a clock for a heart—after being born with severe physical defects. In a society where young people must contribute original research in order to earn their place, Nell struggles to find both her purpose and a sense of belonging. Isolated and longing for a deeper connection than her human relationships can offer, she secretly begins to use banned computers to build an android companion as her research contribution.
title: Spare and Found Parts

abstract: The first novel in The Inheritance Trilogy follows Kare, the son of the cruel and telepathic Empress of a vast galactic empire. As a child, Kare was hidden away on a remote planet by a group of rebels determined to stop the Empress's oppressive rule and prevent her from shaping her son into her successor. Now grown, Kare is torn between the terrifying legacy of his mother’s power and his own desire for freedom and identity. With immense psychic abilities inherited from his parents, he is both a potential weapon and a symbol of hope. As the rebellion gains momentum, Kare must decide whether to embrace his heritage or forge a different path—one that could either save or destroy the galaxy. The novel explores themes of trauma, legacy, free will, and the psychological cost of power.
title: Abendau's Heir

abstract: “The Exile” is a short story that follows the main character, Seán Murphy, who embarks for Luna, the Moon. After seventy years, he decides to go back to Earth and live in Ireland until his death. When he arrives back on Earth, he starts reminiscing about the time his mother found an advertisement asking for people to go work on Luna. Knowing her son would not pass this opportunity for a greater future, she fully supports his decision to immigrate to the Moon, even though she does not want him to leave. He promises to come back for her, but his mother dies after three years working Luna and being promoted to a sort of manager. Seán sees no reason to go back to Ireland and starts to make a life for himself on Luna, marrying and having seven children, who are now dispersed across the solar system. Once he comes back to Ireland years after his wife’s death, he cannot adapt to the weather nor to breathing real oxygen. Seán not only feels uncomfortable but also lonely. Therefore, he returns to Luna, where his friend, also his neighbour, welcomes him back. Seán’s story is about the immigrant experience and searching for the true meaning of home; it is not a place but a matter of personal relationships.

abstract: “Medic” is the first short story in James White’s Hospital Station, the first volume of his Sector General series, taking place sometime before the main narrative in the series, during the construction of Sector Twelve General Hospital. This short story introduces a recurring character of the series, O’Mara. He is suspected to be responsible for an accident during a construction, which causes the death of two alien workers. Whilst he is waiting for the investigation of this accident, the chief sector assigns him to take care of the newly orphaned baby, not because O’Mara is qualified for it, but because the chief sector wants to spite him. Here, White reveals how O’Mara has always been misjudged; despite his tough and muscular appearance, O’Mara is more interested in psychology than construction work. Whilst O’Mara takes care of the alien baby, the narrator chooses to reveal information about the accident step by step, letting the reader form their own prejudices against O’Mara until the truth is fully revealed. Throughout the story, the reader not only learns about O’Mara’s physical and mental abilities but also that he cares a lot more than he lets on like, for example, when he is ready to be crippled in order to save the baby from a rare disease belonging to their species.

abstract:
Amelia Garland Mears’s short story “Mercia, the Astronomer Royal” is set in an imagined future society of the year 2000 which has reverted to the use of Early Modern English. The form of an empire has persisted, but new inventions and discoveries, like the tape recorder and psychic powers, have been integrated into its legal structure and gender equality has nominally been achieved. In this setting, the short story explores the persistence of lingering sexist attitudes and harassment and the challenges faced by women in positions of authority. It follows Mercia, a highly respected female astronomer of the Royal Observatory, who is subjected to unwanted romantic advances from the emperor himself – an act that defies all norms of propriety.
When the emperor visits Mercia’s observatory and she realises his intentions, she firmly implores him to abandon his pursuit. Undeterred, he continues until she is forced to draw her self-defence device, an electrically charged ebony stick customarily carried by many women in the capital. At that moment, her colleague Geometrus unexpectedly returns and interrupts the scene. Humiliated by the rejection and being discovered in a compromising situation, the emperor lashes out. He accuses Mercia of getting into a rage, as is “a woman’s way” and threatening his life. He orders her arrest, leading to preparations for a grand public trial. The news off the incident between the Emperor of the Teutonic Empire and his astronomer spread within hours.
While Mercia is imprisoned, the emperor is overwhelmed by emotions. Still being infatuated with Mercia, he regrets imprisoning her and, refusing to accept her rejection, scrambles to get out of the now messy situation, save face, and still make Mercia his. Torn between embarrassment, anger and lingering desire, he seeks advice from the Dayanand Swami, a sage known for his wisdom and psychic powers, by which he can see snippets of the future. However, the visions of the trial are not what the emperor has hoped for. Ignoring the sage’s warning that attempting to manipulate the future may in fact cause its fulfilment, the emperor sets out to bend the situation to his will.
Meanwhile, Mercia remains steadfast in her integrity and trust that the truth will prevail. Unbeknownst to anyone, Mr. Sadbag, who had fallen asleep behind a folding screen while waiting for an audience with Mercia had witnessed and recorded the entire interaction. On the day of the trial, public speculation runs rampant, but thanks to Mr. Sadbag’s testimony, the truth comes to light. Mercia’s innocence is affirmed, her reputation restored, and the emperor’s misconduct is exposed, leaving his status in ruins. 
Mears's story combines elements of science fiction, social critique, and feminist resistance, making it a strikingly modern work for its time.

title: Mercia, the Astronomer Royal

abstract: This short story is set in a future version of Dublin. The Veracity is a surveilled city where all data is presumed accurate, all behavior monitored, and all deviation treated as threat. The unnamed protagonist is employed as a technician for the Department of Veracity, whose job is to edit, delete or adjust parts of recorded reality to ensure consistency with the official version of the truth. When he stumbles upon minor inconsistencies in the city’s data system, he begins to question the infallibility of the regime - only to discover that manipulation and misinformation are integral to the system itself. The story focuses not on rebellion, but on the quiet, everyday machinery of state-sponsored truth manipulation. It is precisely this bureaucratic normality that makes the dystopia so disturbing. Dublin is not depicted as a violent or chaotic place, but as an orderly society where truth is fluid and centrally managed. Carroll’s depiction of the technician as a calm, obedient worker draws attention to the role of ordinary individuals in maintaining systems of control. The story raises questions about memory, identity, and power. It explores how easily history and reality can be edited when information is digital and centrally stored. The narrative implicitly critiques contemporary tendencies toward information control, surveillance, and revisionism, anticipating debates that have only grown more urgent in the age of big data and algorithmic governance. The ironic title “In Dublin’s Veracity” underlines the core theme: rather than being a city of truth, this future Dublin is one in which truth has become a managed illusion.
title: In Dublin’s Veracity

abstract: This short story is a humorous and satirical take on time travel and art theft, featuring a small group of criminals who plan to steal the Mona Lisa. They have tried this more than just once, by travelling back in time. Their scheme relies on the assumption that multiple copies of the painting can be taken from different historical moments without detection. Therefore, their plan is to go back to the past, take the real painting from the Louvre, and replace it with a perfect copy, so that no one in the present will notice it’s missing. The story is told from the perspective of the narrator, who is part of the team but not fully convinced that everything will go smoothly. As the plan unfolds, things begin to go wrong. The team has underestimated how difficult it is to operate time travel equipment in the field, how unpredictable the past can be, and even how their own copy of the painting might not be as perfect as they thought. They are struggling with basic tasks and making last-minute decisions, that clearly haven’t been thought through. The plot is driven by the tension between clever planning and the chaos that results when time travel is misused. It ends with a comic twist that underlines the absurdity of the plan and the limits of human control over time. The story is also an example of science fiction that draws on art and cultural heritage as part of its speculative premise. By focusing on the Mona Lisa, a universally recognized symbol, Shaw blends high culture with genre fiction in an entertaining and ironic way. The gentle satire becomes obvious within the way the team talks about the Mona Lisa. They see it as just another object to be exchanged, showing little understanding of its cultural values.
title: The Giaconda Caper

abstract: This short story owes its title to Thomas Moore’s poem “Oft, in the Stilly Night”, part of which is featured in the text. It follows the autodiegetic narrator, Mr. Garland, and his wife, Selina Garland, who are currently on bad terms with each other due to Selina’s unexpected pregnancy. On a tight-lipped drive along the Ben Cruachan in Scotland on the way to a holiday, they encounter several farms of the famed slow glass, this short story’s novum. It takes an unusually long time for light to pass through this novelty type of glass, resulting in the display of sceneries it was exposed to months or several years ago. Hoping for a bargain and a distraction from the couple’s pessimistic outlook, Mr. Garland stops the car at a farmhouse advertising slow glass at low prices and high quality. They find the owner, Mr. Hagan, sitting in front of the house, watching a young woman who is looking out the window. He assures that the couple have come to the right place and makes an offer. Although Selina is not convinced, Mr. Garland writes a check. While Mr. Hagan is off to prepare the glass for travel, the narrator notices the young woman and a child playing inside the house. He smiles at them, but they do not seem to notice, leading the narrator to wonder whether they could be blind. When it suddenly starts to rain, Selina rushes to save a rug that Mr. Hagan had laid out for them outside. She opens the door to the farm house to deposit the rug and both she and Mr. Garland catch a glimpse of its insides: The room is cluttered and dirty, so different than what the narrator had seen through the window. The woman and child are nowhere to be seen. The narrator’s terrible suspicion has been revealed to be true: The window is made of slow glass and shows a reality long past. When Mr. Hagan returns, he realizes that the couple has discovered his secret. He tells them that his wife and son were killed in a car accident and returns to his position watching the window from outside.
