title: Light of Other Days

abstract: One morning, protagonist Louise wakes to the unsuspected sight of a pillar above her bed. The short story explores her relationship to the eponymous novum, until the mix-up which has brought it to her is cleared up and the pillar taken away. Pillars are floating assemblages of artificial flames or clouds (at night or during the day, respectively; for high-end models), surrounding and following the owner at all times. Designed for people going through emotionally difficult life phases, they give recommendations for upcoming actions in the owner’s best interest through speech and movement. Louise, a forty-seven year old English teacher, is struggling with a divorce at the time of the pillar’s arrival, but she did not order the pillar. Throughout the story, she discovers the pillar’s positive impacts on her life. She starts succeeding at finishing tasks she struggled with before, like finishing the divorce paperwork and grading papers. She also becomes more active and eventually starts dating through an online platform. On her fourth date with Nigel, who also owns a pillar, she receives a call informing her that there has been a mix-up: Her pillar had been ordered by Martin, her ex-husband, and delivered to his old home. Despite losing her pillar, Louise regains a positive outlook on life through the habits established by the pillar and because of the reassuring information that Martin had, apparently, also been struggling.
container-title: Being Various: New Irish Short Stories
title: Pillars

abstract: A man named Seosamh, who has seemingly been hospitalized in a mental institution, tells the story of how he has ended up in this situation. Seosamh first tells the reader about his neighbor Professor Robert Ó Néill, a nationally renowned scientist who has been attempting to build a machine that allows its users to travel through time. After being invited the protagonist visits the professor who reveals to him that he has achieved his goal and has finally built the Chronotron. As the protagonist is skeptical of the invention, the professor invites him to join him and his engineer for the next ‘ride’. Although he still does not believe the machine to be working, he joins them and soon after finds himself in the year 1921. Ó Néill only then unveils the true purpose of their journey: The atomic destruction of London in order to prevent the Civil War. Seosamh, who clearly does not condone Ó Néill’s plans, tries to talk sense into him, but to no prevail. As soon as the Chronotron reaches London, the professor opens a trapdoor and drops the bomb. As they return to their home Seosamh realizes the professor has vanished. While trying to work out when he could have gone missing he remembers reading about Ó Néill and his birth in London 1921 – accordingly, the destruction of London erased the professor’s existence. The story cleverly plays with the time travel paradox because, until the very end, it is unclear whether Seosamh is mentally ill or whether he is caught is the logical inconsistencies of time travel.
title: The Chronotron

abstract: Set in the Lazaretto of Genoa, two quarantine patients – the unnamed narrator and a German scholar – exchange adventure stories to pass time. In one of these stories the German recounts his own life and his deep fascination with the brain and its matter. In combination with his curiosity about the mythical creation scene in Mary Shelley’s novel Frankenstein, he later becomes fixated on recreating Frankenstein’s fantastic achievement, this time however, granting the creature true consciousness through phrenology, animal magnetism, and galvanism. One night, his tutor Starnstein brings him a disproportional, nameless body. The German seizes the opportunity and decides out of pity to “give the creature a mind” and perfect the original idea of Frankenstein by extracting cerebral gas from cultural icons such as Goethe, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Mezzofanti, and Coleridge and adding them to the creature’s brain to evolve him in different aspects of life. Although he succeeds in his task, the creature despises rather than worships him, as he had initially hoped. The guilt-ridden German admits his mistake and, realizing that he has created a monstrosity, decides to leave for Egypt, guided by a clue he deciphers from a mysterious roll of vellum. Hoping to unravel the mystery, he uncovers – beneath an ancient Egyptian necropolis – a sealed sarcophagus in which lies the body of the “Admit King” whose twitching lips and opening eyes suggest a return from the dead. As the temple begins to shake, demonic figures appear, chanting, while the dead rise from their tombs. As the hideous figures approach the German, he feels an icy, poisonous pain. Then suddenly, emerging from the splitting ground, appears a figure resembling his tutor Starnstein. At that moment, he awakes – revealing that it was all just a dream.
title: The New Frankenstein

abstract: Narrated from an autodiegetic perspective, James Lecky’s story is set during a time of “designer perfection” culture, with rampant cosmetic surgeries and genetic modifications. During this time the renowned Neural sculpture artist Miss Angel McKeown feels creatively stagnant and seeks inspiration for her upcoming collection in Paris. Discovered in a small Dublin gallery by Damien Warbeck, Angel McKeown is now competing in the international art market. In the streets of Istanbul, she purchases hash to escape the artistic pressure but gets involved in a shoot-out which leaves her covered in blood and flesh from the killed drug dealer next to her. The sight of the multiple dead bodies, blood, flesh, bones, and brain matter inspires her to create the so called “Skin-Tight Nightmares” collection. This provocative project uses neural sculptures as pieces of art – crafted from black-market body parts – which are genetically and physically manipulated into grotesque artistic objects. With her neural sculptures, which are best viewed as an art form rather than science, her focus is not on their long-lasting existence but on their artistic impact and spiritual aspect. These living sculptures – mental manipulations of matter – are initially shambling and unconscious of their own existence, and become part of a spiritual and shocking art performance during her Paris exhibition inspired by the violence Angle has seen in Istanbul. She insists on the principle that creation is naturally followed by destruction and Warbeck finally opens the bidding at one million euros.
title: Skin-Tight

abstract: The novella is set in a future European society where memory, language, and geography are tightly controlled by a central authoritarian regime. Ruarí, who works as an apprentice in a state-run agency, is responsible for redrawing maps of the ever-changing landscape, which he later discovers means literally reshaping reality by erasing historical and cultural landmarks from the public consciousness. While he is recording his changes, hills happen to shift or rivers are changing course, and cities appear or vanish unpredictably. His task goes beyond recording these changes, he must understand the forces behind the landscape’s constant transformation. Under the guidance of a master cartographer, Ruari learns to use advanced tools that capture not just static images but the dynamic nature of the terrain. He discovers that maps here don’t merely reflect reality, but they can influence and reshape it. It turns out that each map he creates has its consequences. As Ruarí begins to question the morality of his work, he uncovers forbidden texts and suppressed knowledge that challenge the state's version of truth. His growing awareness of the reality hidden from the people puts him at odds with the regime, leading him to become involved in a resistance movement.
title: The Cartographer’s Apprentice

abstract: The narrator first introduces the secluded living “Professor”, a scientist not by study but by trade. The narrator, one of few people who is in contact with the Professor, visits him in his lonely mansion. It is there where he is shown his latest invention: A device that allows one to look at every place on Earth at all times. As the narrator looks through the device, he is able to see different situations in minute detail. A man in a small town with his family, a family in a small house in the city, a man and a woman in a country they have outgrown, a wealthy man planning to move out of country, and finally a lonely, rich man longing for a small house by the sea in his home country. Making the narrator realize the true nature of the device, he is forced to ask himself the question of the meaning of life.
title: A Vision

abstract: An Irish inventor, namely Cornelius Brayhard, builds a large, steam-powered machine which is a hybrid between a bicycle and an engine that he names Brayhard after himself. Convinced it will revolutionize transportation and secure his fame he launches his prototype. Set in the bustling streets of late 19th-century London, the story traces Brayhard’s attempt to demonstrate the potential of his creation in public. He embarks on a journey through London with the machine, hoping to capture the imagination of the public and the scientific community. However, his hopes for admiration quickly get tarnished. While his invention is impressive in its complexity, it is rather unpractical since it is unstable and difficult to steer. Instead of performing in the anticipated manner, the machine wreaks havoc: it starts to emit smoke and is moves erratically since it is out of control. Pedestrians gather to watch the spectacle while the police intervene and Cornelius and his Brayhard become the center of public attention but not in admiring manner he hoped for. His initial hope to be a crucial part of the scientific revolution turns into a complete disaster.
title: Brayhard

abstract: Set in a world of environmental collapse, a society that is run by orbital elites and where hope is second to power, the novel follows Kai, a systems analyst tasked with developing the infrastructure for floating space-based habitats. Kai is floating somewhat aimlessly through private grief and professional disaffection when she’s sucked into an unfolding conspiracy of digital sabotage, power hierarchies and questions of the ethics of artificially maintained life in orbit. Through a fractured narration that is interspersed with flashbacks and encrypted data fragments, the novel reveals Kai’s troubled history, including her brother’s death and unspoken strife lurking underneath the seemingly utopian orbital society. The main novum in Edge of Heaven isn't any one technology. It is layered, often hidden systems that replicate stability in a world adrift, physically and morally. It asks questions surrounding surveillance, belief, and engineered faith , in both the literal and metaphorical sense, while deliberately obscuring the line between digital facade and spiritual substance. Kelly’s writing is minimalistic in the sense that her sentences are restrained, relying on silence and implication rather than elaborate description , but the conceptual burden of the piece is borne through poetic echoes of silence, cold light, and memory loss. And as Kai gets more enmeshed in the network she thought she was ultimately controlling, the novel raises an uncomfortable question: what does being human mean when survival has been subcontracted to systems?
title: Edge of Heaven

abstract: This brief tale, written during Fitz-James O’Brien’s most intense period of literary activity in the United States, is narrated by a nameless scientist who has succeeded in solving one of the most important natural mysteries: the way to neutralize gravity. A first person scientific confession, the story tells of his discovery and the dangerous experiments that ensue. After building a mechanism to cancel out gravity, he recounts how he feels himself ascending (first indoors, then in a park, and finally into open sky) with more and more amazement and fear. At the core of the story is the novum, the gravity-nullification device, which operates as both a real technological object and as a metaphor for unchecked ambition. In true “mad scientist” tradition, the narrator becomes further alienated from the world below; he is intrigued at the possibility of the “liberation” of humanity from the Earth. The story seeks to create a haunted feeling of disengagement, the narrator’s increasing isolation, and a sense of the disturbing physical sensations of weightlessness. The story can be considered partial forerunner both to the SF of space travel and the psychological horror of liberation from natural laws. Ultimately, the narrator is unsure if he ascended beyond the grip of gravity or was consumed by delusion.
title: How I Overcame My Gravity

abstract: Hospital Station is a collection of five short stories written by James White, which were first published in the New Worlds magazine from 1957 to 1960. In the year 1962 these five short stories were published as an anthology by Ballentine Books. The first short story is titled “Medic” and follows a construction worker called O’Mara who investigates the deaths of two alien construction worker colleagues on a space station construction site and cares for their orphaned infant child. The second short story titled “Sector General” is about Dr. Conway, who begins working at an alien hospital, where he learns about and is confronted with alien anatomy and medical knowledge and acquires advanced technology. The third story, “Trouble with Emily”, follows Dr. Conway as he is assigned to care for a large alien creature resembling a brontosaurus, nicknamed “Emily“. The fourth short story, “Visitor at Large”, features a shapeshifting alien that escapes its treatment; Dr. Conway and his colleague Dr. Prilicla are forced to search for it, all trying to maintain order. In the last short story, “Out-Patient”, Dr, Conway treats an injured alien and is forced to push the boundaries of conventional medicine, using questionable methods. However, in the end he manages to save the patient.
title: Hospital Station

abstract: One day, many months after the sudden disappearance of his father Fintan McHewell, 14-year old Mark McHewell stumbles upon a clue and uncovers a puzzle left behind by his father. Together with the help of his friend Ferdia, they solve the puzzles and find a cubical artifact known as a "tetros". As Mark and Ferdia try to figure out more about the artifact, Mark's friend Niamh is involved in an adventure of her own, soon finding herself abducted and locked up in a lighthouse. Mark eventually frees her and soon the three friends find themselves deeper and deeper in an ever-growing mystery and an ancient conspiracy, involving ancient technology, parallel worlds known as "tirs", a magical and powerful artifact employed by an ancient race of people, and the deaths and disappearances of several friends and foes alike. With the help of the 12 000 year old Del Forgill, they manage to acquire all four "tetroi" and are brought to a different world, which, as the reader learns, is the location of the disappeared Fintan McHewell. Now separated from each other, the book ends with Mark finding himself all alone in an alien world. The book makes great use of the Irish language, many of the terms used, such as “tir”, which means “Land” or “Country”, are Irish words. Other examples found throughout the book are Irish names, such as “Bree” or “Oisin” and terms that describe objects important to the events of the book, such as “sidh”, hills known from Irish mythology, thought to be the home of fairy folk and portals to an “Otherworld”, which is indeed their function in the story.
title: The Magus Conspiracy

abstract:
The rather serious young Irishwoman Nesta McAllister follows her husband Roger to Philadelphia, USA, shortly after the beginning of the truce between the Irish IRA and the British forces. Quiet and reserved by nature, Nesta rarely speaks up and keeps much to herself, until one evening, unlike at previous gatherings, she begins to share a strange and unsettling story. With growing intensity, she recounts a series of dreams she has had: one foretelling her father’s stroke while he was still in good health, and another predicting the drowning of her sister and baby niece aboard the Leinster - both of which came true. While hiding in the mountains of County Cork with her husband, another sequence of dreams haunts her. The first part, once again, comes true; the second, however, remains only partially fulfilled, leaving her in a state of agonizing dread. As her audience listens, half-amused, half-skeptical, Nesta describes a vision of darkness and finality that seems to draw ever closer. The second dream remains unresolved, and the story, as the title promises, ends not with closure, but with the lingering terror of what may still lie ahead. 
Written while Dorothy Macardle was imprisoned in Mountjoy Gaol in 1922 for her anti-Treaty republican activities, the short story reflects a world teetering on the edge of violence. Its conclusion, or lack thereof, hints at the unresolved trauma of civil conflict and the fear of a future still unfolding. In this sense, the story resonates with Irish Science Fiction through its blending of political history and speculative imagination. Dreams and visions function as a kind of science-fictional device, allowing Macardle to explore a future that is both terrifyingly real and suspended in uncertainty, using the supernatural to probe the instability of Ireland´s cultural and political landscape.
title: A Story Without an End (For N.C.)

abstract: Presented as newspaper excerpts from January 1st, 1977, “The Age of Science: A Newspaper of the Twentieth Century” offers a satirical and unsettling glimpse into a future society governed entirely by medical professionals. Written in 1877 under the pseudonym Merlin Nostradamus by Irish journalist and feminist reformer Frances Power Cobbe, the short story cleverly uses a “prospective telegraph”, a kind of time-transcending newspaper, to illustrate how science, once a liberating force, has come to control every facet of human life. In this imagined future, doctors hold all legislative and executive power, and the state’s highest goal is the maximization of health and longevity. Alternative belief systems, such as religion, have been outlawed, and resistance to the scientific regime is met with punishment. Medical experimentation is routinely carried out on animals, particularly dogs and apes, with one report noting that out of approximately 14,000 dogs used in experiments, only 12 survived. While men occupy all positions of power and use science to advance society, women are forbidden from reading or writing, creating a paradoxical blend of scientific “progress” and regressive social control. Cobbe´s tale, while laced with irony and satire, functions as a stinging critique of technocracy, scientific hubris, and the dangers of subordinating moral and individual freedom to institutional authority. Drawing on her background in journalism and activism, particularly her opposition to vivisection and advocacy for women's rights, Cobbe explores how rapid scientific and technological advancements might reshape not only society´s structures but also its fundamental values. Through its speculative lens, “The Age of Science” examines enduring questions about power, progress, and the human cost of so-called rational governance.
title: The Age of Science

abstract:
40 year old Will Carewe has it all — a well-paying job, a beautiful wife — the only thing that is
missing from his 22nd century equivalent of a white picked fence life are children. That, and
immortality. But after the “tie off”, taking the shot that will make one immortal, men lose their libido and ability to procreate. Carewe, who is therefore on the fence of becoming one of the immortal “cool”, is seemingly presented with the perfect opportunity. The pharmaceutical company Farma he works for has cracked the code with E 80, a new version of the immortality drug that supposedly lets men retain their sexual prowess even after the tie off. Carewe doesn’t hesitate to become its first
test subject. But while the procedure is a success, it derails his perfect suburban life quickly. Mysterious accidents threaten his newly acquired immortality, while his already rocky marriage with the wilful Athene deteriorates. The young immortal’s dream of a family comes under fire when his pregnant wife mysteriously disappears. Carewe has to unspool a web of lies and greed at the heart of Farma, before his chance at fatherhood is destroyed forever. Yet his legacy might take on an unexpected shape. According to the blurb, a magazine-published variation of Bob Shaw’s 1970’s novel exists with a somewhat different format and content. The novel version meanwhile deals with questions of immortality and parenthood before the treacherous background of the pharmaceutical industry. Futuristic suburbia meets Golden Age swashbuckling in an exploration of what makes an eternal life truly worth living.
title: One Million Tomorrows

abstract:
Felix Cofie Addy has a bone to pick with Minister Raymond Kuofor of the Fourth Republic. The
fact that he has been dead for three years only makes matters worse. Then again, Ike Okai
Mensah is still mismanaging the FC Maamobi, which might take precedence over Kuofor’s
exploitation of his own people. Meanwhile, Grace Ahulu, pious choirist in life and death, takes a
stance against exploitative Chinese agriculture companies. Most prominently, Faith Anang wants
to have words with her grandson James, Kuofors highly corrupt minister for agriculture. Addy and
the other denizens of Obo Quartey’s digital afterlife Teshie.org band together to complain about potholes on Kanda Highway, rampant corruption and disappointing grandchildren.
Things become uncomfortable very quickly for Quartey and Kuofor’s cabinet. The digitalised dead
turn out to be the Fourth Republic’s undoing, cheered on by their remaining family members. But
not all is what it seems, then the real culprit might be more alive than one might think.
In the background of Ian McDonald’s tongue-in-cheek cyber-futuristic zombie not-apocalypse, a
revolution quietly happens. But that’s really not the important part. Interspersed with anecdotes
about digital necromancer/tech-guru Obo Quartery, McDonald creates a kaleidoscope of
viewpoints from what may or may not lie beyond the pixelated veil. A funny and satirical
exploration of the age-old question of what happens after death, mixed with biting post-colonial commentary and a good helping of grandmotherly disappointment, “A Smart Well-Mannered Uprising of the Dead” is both exactly what it’s title suggests and not at all.
title: A Smart Well-Mannered Uprising of the Dead

abstract: Tony Garnett, the owner of a company that produces special aircrafts, is badly injured when one of his planes crashes onto his car during a test flight. The doctors are able to save him but need to replace a piece of his skull with a metal plate. During his recovery in the hospital, he takes an interest in his beautiful dietician, Janice. As soon as the heavy medication wears off, allowing him to think clearly again, Garnett realizes that he needs to drop his “twenty-metre wing project”. This unprecedented type of wing, which operates with a huge invisible force field, is impossible to sell, as it would drain all the company’s money before meeting the necessary safety requirements. Garnett immediately orders his employee Ian Dermott to stop the project, who grudgingly agrees. Garnett returns to work, but can’t help feeling distrustful of his company. Strange things occur, as the efficiency of certain departments fluctuates unusually, a photograph depicting a piece of the discontinued wing in the background appears, and an employee suffers a sudden form of paralysis. Garnett ascertains that some of his workers were sent to Harlech for a special training course and decides to investigate there himself. Janice, with whom Garnett leads a troubled relationship, accompanies him. The investigation turns out to be futile, so Garnett and Janice have dinner and return to the motel they are staying in. After a fight that causes them to switch their chalets, Janice is killed by a meteorite, hitting the chalet Garnett was supposed to stay in. Convinced that someone attempted to kill him, Garnett confronts Dermott, demanding to know what is going on. Dermott reveals that they are still working on the twenty-metre wing on behalf of extraterrestrials, who are influencing the minds of the people in the company with a device. The metal plate in Garnett’s skull blocks the signal from this device, which is why it occurred to him so suddenly after the accident that pursuing the project made no sense. The extraterrestrials, who have controlled the company from the very beginning, desperately need the wing to repair their spaceship, so they force Dermott to shoot Garnett, who jeopardizes their plan. However, Garnett escapes the attack and manages to get on the shuttle that is supposed to deliver the wing to the aliens. Angry about the death of Janice, Garnett arrives at the spaceship and demands to see their leader so he can kill him. Under the threat that Garnett will destroy the long-awaited spare part, the alien leader reveals himself to him. Garnett is about to kill the alien when a female alien interrupts, who turns out to be Janice. Shortly before Janice died, the extraterrestrials realized their mistake and transferred her consciousness into the body of a female alien. Janice can’t go back to Earth in her new body because it isn’t made for the strong gravity. Therefore, Garnett decides to stay with Janice and the aliens.

abstract: Abe Short is plotting a bank robbery alone in his apartment, when a strange man, whom Abe immediately presumes to be a “mad scientist”, appears in his room. The mad scientist introduces himself as Kincade and ventures to explain that there are two slightly different “timestreams”. Kincade proudly reports that he crossed into an alternative timestream with the help of his “chronomotive device”. Abe steals this device in order to use it for his escape after the robbery, hoping to flee with the money into an alternative reality in which he is not a wanted criminal. Dismissing Kincade’s objections, Abe goes through with his plan and robs the bank. After gaining some distance to the bank building, Abe triggers the device and crosses over into the other timestream, only to run into the alternative version of himself. Once in prison with his other self, Abe finally grasps what Kincade tried to warn him about: the two versions of the world barely differ, at least concerning Abe’s life. Because of this, the other Abe had attempted the same scheme, resulting in the capture of both. The newspaper assumes them to be identical twins but struggles to explain why there is twice as much money as was taken from the bank.

abstract: This collection of poems draws connections between science and poetry, taking inspiration from the life and work of Isaac Newton and other scientific figures. Through inventive use of form and voice, McGovern explores the human side of scientific discovery, often blending historical insight with imaginative speculation. The poems reflect on curiosity, observation, and the costs and consequences of genius, while maintaining an accessible and lyrical style. Though grounded in history and science, the collection also gestures toward the philosophical and emotional dimensions of knowing.
title: The Eyes of Isaac Newton

abstract: In this short story, part of White’s larger Sector General series, a medical space station treats a wide variety of alien life forms with wildly differing physiologies and psychologies. “Custom Fitting” centers on the construction of a specialized spacesuit for a previously unknown alien species whose survival depends on a highly specific environmental configuration. The story showcases White’s trademark optimism and belief in interspecies cooperation, as the medical team races to understand the alien's needs. It combines imaginative xenobiology with a procedural, almost clinical narrative style that emphasizes problem-solving and empathy.
title: Custom Fitting

abstract: Set in the dystopian universe of Judge Dredd, this novel follows the early life of Rico Dredd, a genetic clone and brother of the iconic lawman, as he endures punishment and isolation within the penal colony on Titan, Saturn’s moon. As a prequel narrative, The Third Law reframes Rico not as a villain corrupted by free will, but as a morally ambivalent product of an oppressive, technocratic regime. The novel engages with the conventions of carceral science fiction and space opera, while drawing on cyberpunk aesthetics and dystopian critique. Carroll’s portrayal of Rico’s psychological deterioration, institutional conditioning, and internal rebellion reveals the human cost of authoritarian justice. Science fiction tropes such as genetic engineering, cloning, surveillance technologies, and biopolitical control are central to the narrative, as are themes of moral ambiguity and identity fragmentation. Notably, the story employs a fractured temporal structure, with interwoven memories and retrospective insights that disrupt the chronological flow. This non-linear narration mirrors the protagonist’s disorientation and estrangement from his origins. Within the broader Irish science fiction tradition, Carroll’s work exemplifies how transnational franchises can become vessels for local critique. Although set in an imagined future, the novel implicitly reflects on themes of systemic injustice, institutional alienation, and autonomy concerns that resonate with postcolonial and carceral readings of Irish literature. By reimagining Rico Dredd as a tragic antihero rather than a cautionary figure, The Third Law opens space for empathy, introspection, and resistance within the otherwise rigid moral architecture of the Judge Dredd universe.
title: The Third Law: Rico Dredd – The Titan Years

abstract: Set in post-war Southern Rhodesia, this tale unfolds as a father-son dialogue in a colonial homestead, recounting the father’s traumatic past and his moral awakening. Framed as a deeply personal and reflective conversation, the story combines the lost world and cryptozoological subgenres with imperial adventure fiction. The beast of the title, described as a tragic, dinosaur-like leviathan mourning its dead mate, serves not as a monstrous threat but as a symbol of extinction, memory, and the moral burden of colonial violence. Narratively, the story uses a non-linear structure, interweaving past and present through flashbacks and framed storytelling. Stylistically, it reflects conventions of the colonial memoir and mythic quest but challenges them by replacing conquest with restraint and empathy. The speculative element remains ambiguous, as the narrative leaves it unresolved whether the beast is real, imagined, or allegorical, which deepens the story’s atmosphere of uncertainty and mythic melancholy. The story employs science fiction tropes such as the unknown creature and the exploration of untamed frontiers against a distinctly postcolonial backdrop. The father’s refusal to kill the beast and his insistence that his son vow to do the same stage a generational rejection of violence and dominion. The inclusion of Afrikaans, Dutch expressions, and Biblical allusions further anchors the story in a layered, linguistically hybrid colonial setting. Ultimately, the narrative shifts from imperial spectacle to psychological and ethical reflection, making it an early and compelling example of Irish speculative fiction’s engagement with power, trauma, and ecological loss.
title: The Great Beast of Kafue

abstract: This idiosyncratic narrative unfolds amidst what is proclaimed as “the heaviest snowfall in a century”. The titular character is an agent by profession, an admittedly vague description, situated in contemporary Ireland without any overt elements of an imagined futurity; on the contrary the story is imbued with various undertones of regional specificity, discernible markers of spatial placement. While Scotty ventures outside to find a pub to eat something he encounters an emaciated busker cradling a bodhran drum who asks him for some money to get a meal himself. The absurd and loose plot of the short story unfolds through the protagonist’s growing hypothetical scenarios and borderline fixation with the busker. Sam refrains from helping the poor man and marches towards the pub in the blizzard while the name attains an almost palpable, gelatinous essence in his mind, he seems incapable of letting it slip from consciousness. While enjoying his meal in the pub, he indulges in fictional scenarios of meeting Craig McCathy and decides that he will donate his remaining change; however, “five would have to suffice”. On his way back he does not encounter McCathy, nonetheless he decides to inscribe his name in the snow impulsively. His hands turn bloody from the frenzied effort, and he experiences an almost ecstatic moment, facilitated by the distant and frenetic rhythm of a bodhran drum. After that bizarre incident he runs towards his house deeming this a worthy offering to the street performer who seems affected by this absurd gesture.
container-title: Opulent Syntax: Irish Speculative Fiction
title: Craig McCarthy

abstract:
After experiencing hardship after hardship, from his childhood days to his professional life, Dr. Gervaas Van Varken develops a severe distain for mankind. Being forced into a life as a doctor by his abusive parents and living as an adult under the cruelty of his colleagues on a ship only deepens the man’s misanthropy.
Faced with his hatred, he searches for a solution or answer to his pain and finds possibility in the supernatural teachings of an ancient Tibetan brotherhood. Their chief, a man named Koot Homi, opens up Van Varken’s body and soul to the powers of teleportation, a first step in leaving his mortal existence behind. 
Finally, Van Varken is able to go beyond the borders of human experience and finds himself on a planet known as Hesperos. There he encounters a new kind of civilization, whose inhabitants are immortal and are untouched by religion and gods.
As this novel is structured like a chronicle, it not only describes the life of its protagonist, but also manages to depict a deep and extraordinary history of the Hesperosians and their planet that lays the foundation for the exploration of their unique biology and sociology.
title: History of a World of Immortals without a God

abstract: Queenie, or Caoimhe, is an astro-botanist whose professional expertise and affective relationship with plants has landed her a place in a purposefully vague ecological program related to flora. The story opens in medias res when she begins questioning the condition of her plants and their potential need for some sort of ailment to her cousin Mike; through this interaction several minutiae of this world can be successfully deferred: Ireland is beneath the sea, the Earth has probably been abandoned or decimated, humankind co-inhabits a planet with the Bozar, and people have facilitated an algorithmic society, evidenced by Ro and Goldie, entities with certain android properties. Queenie’s onus is to protect her plants; however, her dismissive boss Bill reassures her that nothing seems particularly alarming, alerting her to the perpetual need for personal improvement in science by resorting to condescending remarks. Later, Queenie eavesdrops on a conversation between him and a mysterious entity, discerning an implied threat towards her life as well as the intention to kill her flora. After a distressing encounter with one of the Bozar, Queenie confides in Mike who takes a protective attitude towards her, implicating their tight familial bond, concomitantly recruiting Ro and Goldie to devise a plan in order to elicit crucial information regarding Bill’s devious plan and potential menace to Queenie.  Following an elaborate ruse set up by the group, the ensuing information seems pedestrian at first; however, Goldie, an “Avarian” who feeds on different kinds of insects, manages to discern a highly irregular pattern regarding the acid produced by certain bees. After corroborating the validity of the information with her mentor Dr Sadbh Morrison and reassuring themselves of the inefficiency of their acidic excretions, they find themselves in the Memorial Park of Queenie’s specimens. One of the bees stings Queenie and she suffers from something akin to an anaphylactic shock, losing her senses. It turns out that Bill had modified these species’ venom, effectively rendering them a chemical weapon highly dangerous for humans, after secretly conniving with the Vespulae, old enemies of the Bozar. In the climactic part of the story, Queenie is recuperating in her hospital bed where the leader of the Vespulae, Consul Vespus, the indelible entity previously conversing with Bill, tries to unsuccessfully murder her following the sudden suppression of its conspiracy, injuring Mike in the process. Its attack is repulsed, and the narrative ends on a positive note, contemplating the strength of familial bonds and the kinship with the non-human.

title: Phosphate Poison

abstract: Thrust in the decrepit, urban landscape of an imagined New York, Mr. Paine works for the enigmatic Agency as a scrubber, a person who can plunge into the psyche of human beings acting as vectors of the “star minnows”. This line of work and the aftermath of these admittedly strenuous experiences result in his abuse of alcohol and persistent insomnia, further conflating his sense of reality and augmenting his hallucinatory outbursts which materialise as lucid dreams, pouring over into the narrative mode, and establishing him as a highly unreliable first-person narrator. Paine shares an intricate bond with Sarah, a cyborg entity also working for the Agency, being able to always communicate telepathically through some sort of cybernetic apparatus. Sarah and Paine shared an intimate romantic relationship before her android transformation; Paine responds to this transhumanist logical endpoint with cynicism and traces of bitterness – mainly because he did not object to it vehemently enough. The Agency superintends its employees via a mode of almost uninterruptible surveillance, attempting to curtail the spread of the “star minnows” virus materially and immaterially through a form of stifling governance relying on the control of information and history. Secondary characters such as Ronnie embody these techno-existential repercussions, their fate reserved for the worst of deaths, corporeal and spiritual. Paine finds himself in a similar situation, experiencing analogous anxieties, plagued by vivid visions of Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons and its alien landscape, the original topos of the “star leeches or minnows” who cascaded to Earth through a 1973 NASA expedition named IcePIC and started utilising human beings as hosts to spread their virus, resulting in mutated, chimerical beings. When the Agency locates such beings, scrubbers consume a highly volatile cocktail of drugs and engage in a psychic communication with the minnows on their Europan form, unmediated by the metamorphosis. This perennial blurring of reality emanates Paine’s persistent musings on the extent of their actions’ efficiency, the inevitability of the minnows’ pandemic spread, the nature of his existence, and the ironic validation of the Fermi paradox in the form of Europa. The question “What did we expect?” reverberates throughout the narrative, culminating in the last dive-in performed by Paine on Roosevelt Island, a place obliquely reserved for the infected. There he is faced with two highly irregular occurrences of mutation, the human brains still intact despite the transmogrification, searching for a Jet Miyake who secretly trespasses there often to provide food and medicine for her parents. Through Paine’s contact with the alien entities and the delusive interaction that ensues, one thing becomes transparent: the reciprocal disappointment of the interspecies mutual effect on one another. Jet is finally tracked down by Paine, bearing the alien virus and promulgating the futility of the Agency’s never-ending hunt. He is unable to kill her, even though he initially recounts the story differently; however, Sarah is there to fulfil her obligation as a delegate of the Agency, informing Paine that he is no longer capable of being a scrubber, perhaps liberating him from this vortex of metaphysical restlessness and self-loathing, or not.
title: Riding the White Bull

abstract:
As an alien quantum engineer, Dr. Quivec has spent most of her adult life researching a new form of instantaneous space travel that could change the known universe and its civilisations forever, as long as the technology is distributed to all. However, after losing her funding, Dr. Quivec finds herself in an illegal strategy/card game with a group of pirates in a pub aboard a space station. Shortly before losing the game, something strikes the station, and in the erupting panic Dr. Quivec is knocked unconscious.
Waking up and finding herself in the deserted pub, save for a few bruised and hungover pirates, she reluctantly agrees to join their crew in order to escape the station with her life. To the group’s dismay, the station’s AI refuses to let its visitors leave. This leads to the crew’s captain, a human woman from Earth, having to blast her way past the station’s locks and armies of robots to reach her crew, allowing them all to escape aboard the pirates’ ship. Already expecting never to be able to finish her research and having to carve out an existence aboard the pirate ship, Dr. Quivec is surprised when she learns that it was the captain’s intention to help her develop the technology all along. Contrary to Dr. Quivec’s beliefs and expectations, the human woman is not a brutal and vicious monster, but a smart former physicist who wants to ensure the technology will be made available to all people of the known universe.
As stereotypes and prejudice remain an unfortunate consequence of human interactions, the perspective is shifted to that of an alien being confronted with her own expectations and preconceptions about humans, which at first might not seem wrong or far-fetched to the reader at all.
title: Captain K'wai'lynn and the Pub of a Thousand Planets

abstract: In Saga, a futuristic city functions as a virtual world whose inhabitants experience as real. Social life is organized through color-coded status cards that determine class, work and access, creating a rigid system of control. Ghost, an airboarder with no memory of the past and no status card, survives through theft and life on the streets. The city is ruled by the Dark Queen, while players from New Earth can enter and leave Saga whenever they want, creating tension between those who can move between worlds and those who are confined within the system. Unlike Epic, the first novel in Kostick’s trilogy, which centers on human players, Saga shifts attention to the inhabitants of the virtual city themselves. In doing so, the novel reflects on what it might mean for created beings to develop consciousness within a world designed for play and how power and inequality can be built into such environments.
title: Saga

abstract: Following the mandate of the World Federation, a galactic expedition is tasked with the colonization of a planet inhabited by the eerily absent Zobranoirundisi. Under rigorous schedules and external pressures, the human party populates the prelapsarian environment under a bluish sun, inhabiting the conspicuously empty houses of the Indigenous peoples while implementing an agricultural policy meant to establish this colony as a “breadbasket planet”. The three main characters embody three distinctly different specializations needed for this endeavour: the unnamed homodiegetic narrator is the commissioning officer, Dunleavy is the engineer, and Martin Chavez is the ecologist, the person responsible for uncovering the true extent of the colonizers’ irreparable ecological mutilation. After ten years spent on this idyllic planet where agrarian economy has been stabilized and most of the agrilogistical problems of the initial stages have been eradicated, effectively terraforming this colony via a production machine of wheat and rye, heavily relying on the sustenance of grazers, the “velvet fields” reveal their true viviparous essence. Chavez realizes that the absence of humanoid forms and the suspicious obliteration of herbivores prior to human colonization is owed to the species existing within the fields, rendering their actions during this ten-year span as the worst genocide ever committed in the World Federation. The aftermath of this dramatic apprehension is equally bleak, as the spasmodic reaction of the colonizers, namely killing all the grazing animals thus committing the same atrocities twice, unfurled the true dramatic irony permeating the narrative. The World Federation condemns the expedition to a similar fate on the hands of the Zobranoirundisi who sprout from their mythical Trees of Life once every hundred years, entitled to reclaim what was so viciously and ignorantly harvested by the colonisers.
